raw_text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|wrenning|6990|wretched}}</noinclude>Stephen’s day, in the north of England, in commemoration of the martyrdom of the saint.

'''wrenning-day''' (ren′ing-dā), ''n.'' St. Stephen’s day, on which wrenning is practised in the north of England.

'''wren-tit''' (ren′tit), ''n.'' A bird, ''Chamæa fasciata'', peculiar to California, of uncertain relations, usually made the type and sole member of a family ''Chamæidæ'': so called from its uniting, to some extent, the habits of a wren and of a titmouse. {{smaller|It is about 6 inches long, with very short rounded wings, a long tail, the beak somewhat like that of a titmouse, the plumage remarkably soft and loose, of a dark-brown color, paler below, and the eye white. See ''Chamæa'' (with cut).}} Also called ''ground-tit''.

'''wrest''' (rest), ''v.''   [< ME. ''wresten'', ''wrasten'', ''wræsten'', < AS. ''wrǣstan'', twist forcibly (cf. AS. ''wrǣst'', firm, strong, = Icel. ''reista'', wrest; cf. Dan. ''vriste'', wrest); prob., with formative ''-t'' (''-tht'' > ''-st''), < ''wrīthan'' (pret. ''wrāth''), writhe, twist: see ''writhe'', and cf. ''wreath''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. also ''wrist'', ''wrestle''.]   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To twist or turn; especially, to deflect, as from the existing or normal state, character, course, or significance: now used chiefly of immaterial things.
{{smaller block|<poem>And finaly he gan his herte ''wreste''
To trusten hire, and tok it for the beste.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, iv. 1427.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>''Wrest'' once the law to your authority:
To do a great right do a little wrong.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', M. of V., iv. 1. 215.}}}}
{{smaller block|The chemists have absurdly, and too literally, ''wrested'' and perverted the elegance of the term microcosm.
{{right|''Bacon'', Physical Fables, ii., Expl.}}}}
'''2.''' To remove, obtain, or bring by or as if by twisting or wringing; extract or pluck with much effort; wring; wrench.

{{smaller block|Thay . . . ''wrast'' out myn yȝen.
{{right|''Alliterative Poems'' (ed. Morris), iii. 80.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>In May, whan the nightyngale
''Wrestes'' out her notes musycall as pure as glas.</poem>
{{right|''Joseph of Arimathie'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 49.}}}}
{{smaller block|Industrious people ''wresting'' a wholesome living out of that stern environment. {{right|''Froude'', Sketches, p. 92.}}}}

'''II.†''' ''intrans.'' To wrestle; contend; strive.

{{smaller block|Thei . . . ''wrested'' against the truth of a long time.
{{right|''Bp. Gardiner'', Of True Obedience, fol. 33. (''Encyc. Dict.'')}}}}

'''wrest''' (rest), ''n.''   [< ME. ''wrest'', ''wreste'', ''wrast''; from the verb.]   '''1†.''' A twist; a writhing.

<poem>First to the ryȝht honde thou shalle go,
Sitthen to tho left honde thy neghe thou cast;
To hom thou boghe withouten ''wrast''.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Babees Book'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 300.}}}}

'''2†.''' A tortuous action; distortion; perversion; hence, a ruse; a stratagem. Compare ''wrench'', ''n.'', 1.

<poem>Than shall we wayte tham with a ''wrest'',
And make all wast that thei haue wroght.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''York Plays'', p. 133.}}}}

'''3.''' An instrument of the wrench, screw-key, or spanner kind; specifically, a key or small wrench for tuning stringed musical instruments, as the harp or piano, by turning the pins to which the strings are fastened. See ''tuning-hammer'', and ''tuning-key'' (under ''key''<sup>1</sup>).

{{smaller block|The Minstrel . . . wore around his neck a silver chain, by which hung the ''wrest'', or key with which he tuned his harp. {{right|''Scott'', Ivanhoe, xliii.}}}}

'''4.''' The partition in an overshot wheel which determines the form of the buckets.   ''E. H.'' {{smaller block|{{right|''Knight.''}}}}

'''wrest-beer†''' (rest′bēr), ''n.'' A kind of beer which, according to Selden, was kept in cellar for a year to mature.

{{smaller block|In brewing of ''Wrest-Beer'', there ’s a great deal of business in grinding the Mault. {{right|''Selden'', Table-Talk, p. 81.}}}}

'''wrest-block''' (rest′blok), ''n.'' In the pianoforte, a wooden block, often made of several pieces, into which the wrest-pins are driven. It is of great importance in securing permanence of tune and sonority of tone. Also called ''pin-block'', ''back-block'', ''wrest-plank.''

'''wrester''' (res′tėr), ''n.''   [< ''wrest'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.]   One who wrests or perverts.

'''wrestle''' (res′l), ''v.''; pret. and pp. ''wrestled'', ppr. ''wrestling.''   [Also formerly or dial. ''wrastle'', Sc. ''warstle''; < ME. ''wrestlen'', ''wrastlen'', ''wrastelen'', ''wrystellen'', < AS. ''wræstlian'', wrestle (rare), the form more commonly found being ''wraxlian'' (> ME. ''wraxlen'', ''wrasklen'') = OFries. ''wraxlia'' = MD. ''wrastelen'', ''worstelen'' = MLG. ''wrostelen'', ''worstelen'', LG. ''wrosseln'', ''worsteln'', wrestle; freq. of ''wrest.'']   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1†.''' To twist or wind about; especially, to writhe; wriggle; squirm; struggle, as with the limbs.

{{smaller block|Petrius peyned hym sore to a-rise and turned ''wrastelinge''; but all that availed not. {{right|''Merlin'' (E. E. T. S.), iii. 655.}}}}
{{smaller block|From hence the river having with a great turning compasse after much ''wrestling'' gotten out towards the North. {{right|''Holland'', tr. of Camden, p. 279. (''Davies.'')}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>And aye she ''warsled'', and aye she swam,
Till she swam to dry land.</poem>
{{right|''The Water o’ Wearie’s Well'' (Child’s Ballads, I. 200).}}}}
'''2.''' To struggle in a hand-to-hand contest; strive, as for some advantage or for mastery, with bodily strength and adroitness; specifically, to struggle, as two persons striving to throw each other to the ground, especially in a contest governed by certain fixed rules.
{{smaller block|<poem>For many a man that may not stonde a pul,
It liketh hym at ''wrastelyng'' for to be.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Parliament of Fowls, l. 165.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Wrothely thai wrythyne and ''wrystille'' togederz.</poem>
{{right|''Morte Arthure'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 1141.}}}}
{{smaller block|And Jacob was left alone; and there ''wrestled'' a man with him until the breaking of the day. Gen. xxxii. 24.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>You have ''wrestled'' well, and overthrown
More than your enemies.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', As you Like it, i. 2. 266.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Each one may here a chooser be,
For room ye need not ''wrastle.''</poem>
{{right|''Drayton'', Nymphidia.}}}}
Hence—'''3.''' To contend in any way, as in a struggle for mastery; maintain opposition or resistance, especially against a moral foe or force; strive.
{{smaller block|<poem>I persuaded them, if they loved Benedick,
To wish him ''wrestle'' with affection,
And never to let Beatrice know it.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Much Ado, iii. 1. 42.}}}}
{{smaller block|Put on the whole armour of God that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil, for we ''wrestle'' not against flesh and blood but against spiritual wickedness.
{{right|Eph. vi. 12.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>’Twill be some pleasure then to take his Breath,
When he shall strive, and ''wrestle'' with his Death.</poem> ''Cowley'', Davideis, i.}}

'''4.''' To deal, as with a troublesome duty; apply one’s self vigorously; grapple: as, to ''wrestle'' with a knotty problem; to ''wrestle'' with a distasteful task. [Colloq.]—'''5.''' Hence, to devote one’s self earnestly to prayer; pray. [Cant.]
{{smaller block|<poem>My reverend Clergy, look ye say
The best of thanksgiving ye ha’e,
And ''warstle'' for a sunny day.</poem>
{{right|''Scott'', Carle, now the King’s Come, ii.}}}}

'''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To contend with in wrestling: as, I will ''wrestle'' you for so much. [Colloq.]—'''2.''' On a cattle-range, to throw for the purpose of branding, as an animal. [Slang, western U. S.]
{{smaller block|A fire is built, the irons heated, and a dozen men dismount to, as it is called, ''wrestle'' the calves.
{{right|''T. Roosevelt'', The Century, XXXV. 861.}}}}

'''wrestle''' (res′l), ''n.''   [Also dial. ''wrastle''; < ''wrestle'', ''v.'']   A bout at wrestling; a wrestling-match.
{{smaller block|Corineus, . . . whom in a ''wrestle'' the giant catching aloft, with a terrible hugg broke three of his ribs.
{{right|''Milton'', Hist. Eng., i.}}}}
{{smaller block|If he had gone out for a few days with his sinewy cousins in the country, and tried a ''wrastle'' with one of them, he would have quickly found that his body was a pretty slim affair. {{right|''Tribune Book of Sports'', p. 5.}}}}

'''wrestler''' (res′lėr), ''n.''   [< ME. ''wrastlare'', wrestler; < ''wrestle'' + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' One who wrestles; specifically, one who makes a practice of wrestling, as a professed athlete.
{{smaller block|Was not Charles, the duke’s ''wrestler'', here to speak with me? {{right|''Shak.'', As you Like it, i. 1. 94.}}}}

'''2.''' One who wrestles cattle on a range. [Slang, western U. S.]
{{smaller block|The calf-''wrestlers'', grimy with blood, dust, and sweat, work like beavers. {{right|''T. Roosevelt'', The Century, XXXV. 861.}}}}

'''wrestling''' (res′ling), ''n.''   [Verbal n. of ''wrestle'', ''v.'']   The act of trying to throw another person to the ground; the act of two persons contending which shall throw the other to the ground and overpower him. {{smaller|Wrestling, as a game subject to special rules, is of great antiquity. It was held in high esteem by the Greeks, and their youth were taught it by special masters as part of the public education. In its highest and simplest form it was the fifth of the five tests of the pentathlon. In this contest the wrestlers wrestled standing and naked, any hold being allowed, and three falls constituting victory. Wrestling, in combination with boxing, formed the arduous and dangerous contest known as the ''pancratium''—a contest much more resembling a fight to a finish than an athletic contest. A third form of wrestling, which does not seem to have come down to modern times, consisted in interlocking the fingers, pushing the palms of the hands together, and twisting the joints and wrists, without the assistance of any other member or of any hold of the body. The highest and purest form of Greek wrestling does not appear to have been transplanted to Rome, although the more contentious and cruel pancratium—a sport more nearly allied to the Roman gladiatorial spirit—was introduced there by Caligula, and became very popular.}}
{{smaller block|Go not to the ''wrastelinge'', ne to scholynge at cok. {{right|''Babees Book'' (E. E. T. S.), p. 40.}}}}

'''wrest-pin''' (rest′pin), ''n.'' In the pianoforte and harp, a steel pin driven into the wrest-block or frame, around which one end of a string is wound, and by turning which the string may be tuned; a tuning-pin. {{smaller|The upper part of the pin is square in section, so as to be turned by a tuning-hammer or -key. See cut under ''harp.''—'''Wrest-pin piece,''' in the pianoforte, a metal plate through which the wrest-pins are screwed into the wrest-block.}}

'''wrest-plank''' (rest′plangk), ''n.'' Same as ''wrest-block.''

'''wretch''' (rech), ''n.'' and ''a.''   [< ME. ''wrecche'', ''wrechche'', ''wræcche'', ''wrehche'', < AS. ''wrecca'', ''wræcca'', ''wreca'', outcast, exile (= OS. ''wrekkio'', an adventurer, warrior, = OHG. ''wreccho'', ''reccho'', a banished man, exile, stranger, adventurer, MHG. G. ''recke'', a warrior, hero, giant), lit. ‘one driven out’; cf. ''wræc'', exile, < ''wrecan'', drive out, banish, persecute, avenge, wreak: see ''wreak''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''I.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' A very miserable person; one who is in a state of desperate unhappiness or misfortune, or is exposed to unavoidable suffering or disgrace.
{{smaller block|<poem>I ''wrecche'', which that wepe and waille thus,
Was whylom wyf to King Capaneus.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Knight’s Tale, l. 73.}}}}
{{smaller block|Fly, ye ''Wretches'', fly, and get away, for your King is slain.
{{right|''Baker'', Chronicles, p. 15.}}}}
{{smaller block|The poor ''wretch'', half dead with fear, expected every moment to fall by the bloody hands of the Djawi.
{{right|''Bruce'', Source of the Nile, II. 590.}}}}
'''2.''' A sorry or contemptible creature; a despicable person: a term of opprobrium applied to one who has incurred condemnation by misconduct, and often used on slight occasion and with little intended force.

{{smaller block|<poem>Fie on thee, ''wretch!'' ’tis pity that thou livest
To walk where any honest men resort.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', C. of E., v. 1. 27.}}}}
{{smaller block|Does not every dowager in London point to George Fitz-Boodle as to a dissolute ''wretch'' whom young and old should avoid?
{{right|''Thackeray'', Fitz-Boodle’s Confessions.}}}}
'''3.''' Body; creature; thing: used (in some manner that indicates the intention) of a person regarded with some degree of kindly or ironical commiseration, or, when genuine words of endearment seem inadequate, with tender sympathy or passion, or even with admiration.
{{smaller block|<poem>Excellent ''wretch!'' Perdition catch my soul,
But I do love thee!</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Othello, iii. 3. 90.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Poor ''wretch'' was never frighted so.</poem>
{{right|''Drayton'', Nymphidia, st. 27.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Come forth,
Fond ''wretch'', and know thyself and him aright.</poem>
{{right|''Shelley'', Adonais, xlvii.}}}}
'''II.'''† ''a.'' Miserable; wretched.
{{smaller block|Thu ''wrecche'' wiht.
{{right|''Owl and Nightingale'', l. 556.}}}}

'''wretchcock†''', ''n.'' See ''wretchock.''

'''wretched''' (rech′ed), ''a.''   [< ME. ''wrecched'', ''wreched'', ''wriched'', wretched, miserable; < ''wretch'' + ''-ed''<sup>2</sup>. For the form, cf. ''wicked''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' Suffering from or affected by extreme misery or distress; deeply afflicted; miserable; unhappy.
{{smaller block|Thir wormes ete that ''wreche'' [var. ''wreched''] manne.
{{right|''Old Eng. Metr. Homilies'' (B), l. 215. (''Morris and Skeat.'')}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>I am, my lord, a ''wretched'' Florentine.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', All’s Well, v. 3. 158.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>O ''wretched'' husband of a ''wretched'' wife!
Born with one fate, to one unhappy life!</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Iliad, xxii. 608.}}}}
{{smaller block|All his life long he had been learning how to be ''wretched'', as one learns a foreign tongue.
{{right|''Hawthorne'', Seven Gables, x.}}}}
'''2.''' Characterized by or causing misery or unhappiness; very afflicting, annoying, or uncomfortable; distressingly bad in condition or relation: as, the ''wretched'' condition of a prison; ''wretched'' weather; a ''wretched'' prospect.
{{smaller block|<poem>Unhappy, ''wretched'', hateful day!</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', R. and J., iv. 5. 43.}}}}
{{smaller block|It was not merely during the three hours and a half which Uncle Sam claimed as his share of my daily life that this ''wretched'' numbness held possession of me.
{{right|''Hawthorne'', Scarlet Letter, Int., p. 39.}}}}
{{smaller block|The ''wretched'' business of warfare must finally become obsolete all over the globe.
{{right|''J. Fiske'', Amer. Pol. Ideas, p. 151.}}}}
'''3.''' Of miserable character or quality; despicable; contemptible; reprehensible; strongly objectionable: used of persons or things: as, a ''wretched'' blunderer or quibbler; a ''wretched'' quibble; ''wretched'' stuff.
{{smaller block|<poem>Safe where no critics damn, no duns molest,
Where ''wretched'' Withers, Ward, and Gildon rest.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Dunciad, i. 296.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>At war with myself and a ''wretched'' race.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Maud, x. 2.}}}}
'''4.''' Worthless; paltry; very poor, mean, inefficient, unsatisfactory, unskilful, or the like: as, a ''wretched'' poem; a ''wretched'' cabin; a ''wretched'' defense or piece of work.
{{smaller block|<poem>Affected noise is the most ''wretched'' thing
That to contempt can empty scribblers bring.</poem>
{{right|''Roscommon'', Translated Verse.}}}}
{{smaller|='''Syn. 1.''' Forlorn, woebegone.—'''3.''' Vile, sorry, shabby, pitiful.}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
